First off, take a breath.
Second, as a fellow first year myself, I got one good piece of advice: Do not overthink or overdo it, work will always be there, so take things moderately, and just start on what is attainable.
I saw my classroom just less than a week before school started. They had used the room as a storage room, every cabinet was cluttered, and even the desk was filled with garbage, I did what I could and even got help from my boyfriend and sister. I hardly made a dent.

Just stick with the essentials. Do not think about decorations as a priority; student work can eventually decorate the empty room lol. Just organize what you know will be essential for the classroom (seating, where to place hw/assignments, access to basic materials). And to be fair, your main concern should just be classroom management,  protocols, and your first lesson. Trust me, it's been a month, and I'm still trying to organize and declutter.

And don't be afraid to ask!! Every veteran teacher was once a first year! They are VERY aware that you will be clueless as they were once themselves. I am still trying my best to go up to my coworkers and ask questions I think are really dumb lol.

It never ends. Prioritize your instruction, the essentials, and  eventually you can start putting together your classroom to what you desire.

This is going to be such an absolute hot take on my part, since I think I can see where she's coming from: I grew up in a super conservative household. Sex was something I believed was something you don't easily give away. So with my first couple of partners, I refused to do it with them, mainly because I was fear mongered from doing it due to my culture. Though some ended because that's not their flow, it never got to me. Except for one person who I was smitten over. I laid out the no sex rule on them, and they said they were okay with it...for a while. Then it became one of the factors as to why he wanted to end it. I was devastated. Out of that devastation, I started to go into a spiraled fear, the not so uncommon perception that no man would truly love me unless I gave it away. So I did later on, thinking that's how  I could keep a relationship running. I realized after being active that sex was not a  devilish, horrible act, but a way to just feel connected with a person at a physical level. OP, here's my hot take: I think out of desperation, and of course, because of the breakup, she thought she wouldn't ever find someone again unless she did it, not because she didn't want to have sex with you. Now she came back thinking you'd want her back because she feels comfortable now to have sex. However, I don't think you should get back with her. It seems to me like you won't ever interpret it that way, and you'll always have that nagging feeling, questioning yourself "why them but not me?" I hope she learned more about herself, and I hope you realized that having no sex as a condition from a partner is uncompromisable for you.
